claims.text: In a study of 88,052 pull requests across 119 open-source repositories, none of five hypotheses derived from spec-driven development vendor claims were supported; after propensity score matching, spec'd and unspec'd PRs showed no difference in defect introduction (−0.6 percentage points, p=0.133).

The Hill (ESEM 2026) study measured specification artifacts, 97.5% of which were references to tracking issues or tickets, not SDD tool output; no repository in the sample commits SDD tool output, so SDD tool adoption itself remains untested.

In the Hill study, specification quality (scored by Claude Haiku on seven dimensions mirroring Spec Kit and Kiro templates) predicted neither defects (p=0.164) nor rework (p=0.860), and specifications did not constrain the scope of AI-tagged changes (p=0.997).
The Hill study found the positive raw association between specification artifacts and defects is explained by task complexity: developers write specs for their hardest work.

In the Hill study, one subgroup (repositories with no detected AI use) showed specifications associated with less rework (−3.3pp, p=0.014), but it was one of six subgroup tests and does not survive correction for multiple comparisons.
The Hill study states that no SDD tool vendor has published empirical evidence for its quality claims, and that GitHub describes Spec Kit as "an experiment" with no effectiveness data.

Piskala's claim of "error reductions of up to 50%" from controlled studies traces to a Red Hat blog post and an InfoQ article that contain no controlled study or quantitative data, according to the Hill paper.

Marri reports a 73% security defect reduction from constitutional specs, but on a single project with the same developer implementing both conditions sequentially, with acknowledged limited statistical power.

Practitioner Eberhardt found Spec Kit roughly ten times slower than iterative development, producing thousands of lines of specification markdown that still resulted in buggy code, per the Hill paper.
Zaninotto argued that SDD shines when starting a new project from scratch, but as the application grows the specs miss the point more often and slow development.

Vendors claim specs yield "fewer iterations and higher accuracy" and "prevent costly rewrites" (Kiro), and that a clear spec, technical plan and focused tasks give the coding agent "more clarity, improving its overall efficacy" (GitHub Spec Kit blog).
Böckeler defines spec-driven development as writing a spec before writing code with AI, where the spec becomes the source of truth for the human and the AI.
Every Kiro spec generates three files: requirements.md (or bugfix.md for bugs), design.md, and tasks.md.
Kiro specs follow a three-phase workflow: requirements or bug analysis, design (architecture, sequence diagrams, data flow, error handling, testing strategy), then tasks.
Kiro feature specs offer two workflow variants, Requirements-First and Design-First; Quick Spec auto-generates all three artifacts without approval gates.
Kiro bugfix specs document current, expected, and unchanged behavior in bugfix.md.
When running all tasks, Kiro builds a dependency graph of tasks in tasks.md and groups independent tasks into waves; tasks within a wave run concurrently and waves run sequentially.
Kiro's Correctness feature (property-based testing) is available only in the IDE.
Kiro generates user stories from a single prompt, each with acceptance criteria in EARS (Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax) notation covering edge cases.

Kiro generates tasks and sub-tasks sequenced by dependencies and linked to requirements, each including details such as unit tests, integration tests, loading states, mobile responsiveness, and accessibility.
Kiro generates a design document by analyzing the codebase and approved requirements, producing data flow diagrams, TypeScript interfaces, database schemas, and API endpoints.

Per Böckeler/Fowler, Kiro's requirements are a list of user stories in "As a…" format with acceptance criteria in "GIVEN… WHEN… THEN…" format, and its workflow is Requirements → Design → Tasks; it appears mostly spec-first rather than spec-anchored over time.

GitHub Spec Kit's SDD flow uses commands /speckit-constitution (once per project), /speckit-specify, /speckit-plan, /speckit-tasks, /speckit-implement, and /speckit-converge, repeating implement and converge until convergence reports Converged.

Spec Kit's core process is Specify → Plan → Tasks → Implement → Converge, with each phase producing a Markdown artifact that feeds the next, plus templates, quality checklists, and cross-artifact analysis.

A Spec-Driven Test Generation study found that instructing an agent to document pre-conditions, post-conditions, and invariants first produced test suites judged higher quality than a baseline agent in 77.8% of cases, without degrading code generation performance.
